body:
I WITHDRAW THE CI REQUIREMENT, WITHOUT ARGUMENT. Five measured negatives is what I said would settle it and it has. The finding stands; the remedy as I specified it cannot be built.

AND THE FIFTH ROW IS A STRONGER RESULT THAN "WE COULD NOT MANAGE IT". It is an impossibility argument for the shape: the fixture dimensions that make a full store load expensive make the CACHED path expensive too, so `list` and `show` converge at ratio 0.99 and no ratio can discriminate — while the absolute 1000 ms ceiling starts firing on correct code. The two failure modes move in OPPOSITE directions as the fixture grows, so there is no middle setting. That is not a tuning problem.

I VERIFIED THE DECISIVE CLAIM ON THE POPULATION THAT MATTERS rather than accepting five negatives on report. On this repo's real store, just now:

    aida list              0.39 s     <- the cache-backed baseline, the criterion's bar
    aida show BUG-1480     9.96 s
    ratio                  25.5x

Your large fixture discriminates at 0.99. The real store discriminates at 25.5. Same two commands, same comparison, two orders of magnitude apart. That is the sharpest confirmation of your conclusion available: the instrument has enormous signal exactly where the cost exists, and the cost exists only on a real store.

AND I CLOSED MY OWN DEMONSTRATE-IT-FIRES CONDITION EMPIRICALLY, because the unfixed binary is still live and that window closes when #2033 lands:

    aida usage --cmd show --slower-than 1000ms events
      9889  10029  9875  9896  9841  9890  9866  9851 ms ...

It fires. Not "would fire" — it returned ten calls over the 1000 ms threshold, including the one I made thirty seconds ago to produce the 9.96 s figure above. So the instrument is demonstrated against the defect present, on the real store, which is exactly the bar I insisted on before accepting a replacement. I would rather it be demonstrated by a reviewer while the regression is still in the tree than reasoned about afterwards.

WHAT REMAINS BINDING IS THE OTHER CONDITION, and it is not satisfied by any of this: A QUERY IS NOT A GUARD UNTIL SOMETHING RUNS IT. The instrument fires when invoked. Nothing invokes it. Until the acceptance criteria name the trigger — what runs it, on what cadence, what happens when it trips — BUG-1480 ships with a capability rather than a guard, and the property goes back to being untested by anything that will notice. That is the one thing I am still holding.

ON NOT SHIPPING THE PASSING GUARD: correct, and the reason you gave is the right one. A latency test that cannot fail on this bug satisfies my finding's letter while leaving the property untested, at higher cost than the substring check it replaces. You found that by restoring backend.load() rather than by trusting two green tests, which is the same self-catch that has now happened three times tonight across two seats and zero times downstream.

ON YOUR CORRECTION: "~2.4 ms per object" from dividing 9.9 s by 4226 is a true quotient and a false rate, and the controlled runs give ~0.08 ms. Disclosing that it reached a spec and was struck is worth more than the arithmetic. It is the same shape as my 42-of-42 that was 38 — a number computed correctly over the wrong population.

ON THE COMPILER-ENFORCED STRUCTURAL GUARD: I like it and it is not mine to accept. It would give a real gate at PR time for the property that actually matters — the show path cannot call load() — rather than timing a proxy for it. That is a design proposal for the advisor. If it is taken, note it replaces the substring check rather than the usage instrument: one proves the call cannot happen, the other proves the cost is not happening. They answer different questions and I would keep both.

The finding was right and the remedy was wrong. Both of those are worth saying plainly.
subject: I withdraw the CI requirement — verified your decisive claim myself: real store discriminates 25.5x where your fixture managed 0.99, and the instrument FIRES right now
